criterion_notes.c1: Examines urban potable water supply service access across 172 municipalities in Pernambuco, Brazil, focusing on household economic accessibility (water tariff affordability for residential-social and residential-non-social households) and water consumption/demand.
criterion_notes.c2: Satisfies BOTH the plain wording of Criterion 2 and the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type mechanism reading. Under the plain wording, the study examines water utility tariff regulation and public-utility financial governance. Under the narrow 2026-10-13 reading, tariff and cost-recovery rules directly governing service access—specifically regulated municipal water tariff levels, social tariff categorization (households earning below vs. above one monthly minimum wage), and state utility cost-recovery constraints—are explicitly enumerated rule-type mechanisms.
criterion_notes.c3: Contains empirical analysis using 2010 municipal-level administrative, operational, and census data for 172 municipalities (1,805,405 active connections) from COMPESA (obtained via Access to Information Law), SINISA, and the IBGE Demographic Census to evaluate observed 2010 tariff affordability and cost recovery and calibrate a multi-objective nonlinear programming (NLP) tariff optimization model. Note that while simulated Pareto-frontier counterfactuals lack statistical standard errors for meta-analysis, Criterion 6 of INCLUSION_EXCLUSION.md specifies that quantitative effect-size extractability is a synthesis gate rather than a systematic-review inclusion gate.
criterion_notes.c4: Reports service-access outcomes directly relevant to affordability and quantity: (1) household water bill affordability measured against a 3%-of-household-income benchmark (squared affordability gap OF2 and number of municipalities where residential-social and residential-non-social bills exceed, equal, or fall below 3% of income under observed 2010 tariffs and optimized tariffs) and (2) quantity of potable water demanded/billed across consumer categories.
criterion_notes.c5: Population and unit of analysis (172 municipalities in Pernambuco served by COMPESA, covering 1,805,405 active water accounts across 5 user categories, analysed at the municipality-by-user-category level and aggregated to 12 Development Regions), exposure (observed 2010 COMPESA tariff regime vs. Pareto-optimal water tariffs and cost-recovery targets across social and non-social categories), outcome (household water affordability relative to 3% income threshold, water volume demanded, and utility net revenue), and study design (cross-sectional empirical municipal analysis combined with calibrated multi-objective nonlinear optimization modeling) are all clearly specified.
criterion_notes.c6: Full text is published in English (with English and Portuguese title and abstract), which is eligible without translation.

evidence_quotes.quote: The model, applied to 172 municipalities in Pernambuco using 2010 data from a major water utility, was designed to optimize two conflicting objectives: enhancing financial viability through improved net revenue and ensuring tariff affordability for consumers.
For average income data, households earning less than one monthly minimum wage were classified as residential-social, while those earning more were considered residential non-social.

Increasing block tariff (IBT) structures and social tariff mechanisms are often designed to reconcile financial sustainability with the recognition of access to water as a fundamental human right. In this context, the results of the model should not be interpreted as prescribing specific tariff increases, but rather as illustrating the potential trade-offs that regulators face when balancing cost recovery and the protection of vulnerable consumers eligible for social tariffs.

operational and financial indicators from the sanitation sector were sourced from the National Sanitation Information System (SINISA); consumer-type data, such as the number of active connections, average tariffs, and volumes consumed and billed by user category, were obtained directly from COMPESA (through a request submitted via access to information law); and socioeconomic information was collected from the IBGE Census

The other objective function represents the sum of the squared differences between the water bill paid by a representative consumer and their affordability level across all municipalities (a function to be minimised). This objective function can be understood as an equity measure.

The optimal results indicate that an increase in tariffs is, as expected, associated with a reduction in water consumption. This outcome may contribute to improved service provision by alleviating pressure on the limited water supply and by enhancing financial capacity, thereby enabling investments, including those required for the universalization of water supply and sanitation services.

raw_response.exposure: Regulated potable water tariff levels and cost-recovery rules across five consumer categories (including residential-social vs. residential-non-social differentiation), comparing COMPESA's actual 2010 tariffs with Pareto-optimal multi-objective tariff schedules
raw_response.outcome: Household water tariff affordability (squared deviation between water bill and the 3%-of-household-income affordability threshold, plus count of municipalities where bills exceed 3% of income), quantity of potable water demanded/billed, and utility net financial balance (revenue minus cost)
raw_response.population_and_sample: 172 municipalities in Pernambuco, Brazil served by the state-owned utility COMPESA in 2010, encompassing 1,805,405 active water connections across five user categories (residential-social, residential-non-social, commercial, industrial, and public) aggregated into 12 Development Regions (unit of analysis: municipality-by-consumer-category, aggregated to municipality and Development Region)
raw_response.rationale: This English-language empirical and calibrated multi-objective optimization study examines potable water tariff and cost-recovery rules across 172 municipalities in Pernambuco, Brazil (1,805,405 active COMPESA connections) using 2010 SINISA, COMPESA administrative records, and IBGE Census household income data. It directly evaluates tariff and cost-recovery rules—including social residential (<1 minimum wage) versus non-social residential tariff differentiation—which is an explicitly listed rule-type mechanism under both the plain wording and the 2026-10-13 narrow clarification of Criterion 2. It reports both observed 2010 and Pareto-optimal outcomes for household water affordability (relative to the 3%-of-income benchmark, including the number of municipalities exceeding the threshold) and water quantity demanded, satisfying all systematic-review inclusion criteria (c1–c6).
raw_response.study_design: Cross-sectional empirical municipal assessment (2010 administrative and census data) combined with a calibrated multi-objective nonlinear programming (NLP) optimization model
